title: India Tells Washington Its Forced Labour Tariff Case Has No Evidence. The Hearing Got Personal.
excerpt: At the USTR's Section 301 hearings, India's government and industry groups dismantled the case for a 12.5 per cent duty — while a ticking clock on July 24 makes the fight existential.
body:
India's government and its top industry bodies pushed back forcefully this week at public hearings in Washington, challenging the United States Trade Representative's proposal to impose a 12.5 per cent tariff on Indian goods under Section 301 of the Trade Act.

The USTR launched the investigation in March, accusing 60 economies — including India, China, Japan, Australia and the United Kingdom — of failing to prevent goods produced with forced labour from entering global supply chains. Its findings, released on June 3, proposed additional tariffs of 10 to 12.5 per cent on imports from 54 of those economies.

## India Calls the Evidence Thin

James Nedumpara, head of the Centre for Trade and Investment Law established by India's commerce ministry, testified on behalf of the government. He argued that the USTR's findings applied a sweeping, one-size-fits-all assessment to dozens of countries without providing India-specific evidence of harm.

"India submits that a mere absence of a forced labour import prohibition, without meeting the evidentiary basis of other statutory requirements, cannot be construed as 'unreasonable' within the meaning of Section 301 of the Act," the government's submission stated.

India cited its ratification of two International Labour Organization conventions on forced labour, its constitutional prohibition on trafficking and forced labour under Article 23, and its enforcement mechanisms against both state and private actors.

## Industry Groups Warn of Collateral Damage

Poornima Shenoy, representing the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry in the United States, told the USTR panel that the tariffs would ultimately punish American consumers and businesses rather than addressing forced labour.

"An additional tariff will increase costs not only for Indian exporters, but also for US manufacturers, importers, retailers and ultimately American consumers," Shenoy said. "Higher tariffs for these established supply chains will raise costs for businesses that already follow compliance standards."

Suchita Sonalika of the Confederation of Indian Industry argued that India's policy framework does not qualify as "unreasonable" or "discriminatory" under the statute, and that the USTR had failed to demonstrate measurable harm to American industry.

## A Tariff Replacement, Not a New Idea

The hearings carry special urgency because the proposed duties are widely seen as an effort to replace a temporary 10 per cent tariff imposed in February after the Supreme Court struck down President Donald Trump's broad global tariffs under an emergency law. Those interim duties expire on July 24, giving the USTR only days to finalise a new framework.

Twenty-two attorneys general from Democratic states filed their own objections on Monday, calling the forced labour tariffs "an attempt to paper over predetermined sweeping tariffs" and warning of a potential court challenge.

## The Trade Deal That Was Supposed to Be Done by Now

The timing compounds pressure on a separate track: the India-US bilateral trade deal that Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal said would be finalised by mid-July. That deadline is now here, but the Section 301 investigation has complicated negotiations.

An Indian trade official said last month that the deal could only be finalised after the USTR investigation concludes, with New Delhi seeking an assurance from Washington that it will not face additional tariff hikes after any agreement is signed.

Wendy Cutler of the Asia Society Policy Institute described the challenge bluntly: "Each side has its own priorities and redlines which continue to prevent a successful conclusion. Moreover, developments over the last year have produced a serious trust deficit on the part of Delhi."

## What This Means for the Diaspora

For the roughly 4.4 million Indian Americans and the broader network of Indian professionals and businesses in the United States, the stakes are direct. A 12.5 per cent tariff on Indian goods would raise costs across sectors from textiles and pharmaceuticals to auto components and chemicals.

Indian IT services companies, which employ hundreds of thousands of workers in the United States, operate within supply chains that could see cascading cost increases. Small and mid-sized Indian exporters — already navigating a strong dollar and weak global demand — would face margins thin enough to force some out of the US market entirely.

India's government has signalled it will continue to contest the tariffs through the USTR's post-hearing rebuttal process. But with the July 24 expiry of existing duties fast approaching, the window for resolution is narrow.
